name: Eyebrow growth serum

lead: Eyebrow growth serums are topical products, often containing peptides or botanical extracts, sold to make sparse brows look denser and fuller. Fuller brows frame the eyes and strengthen the upper face.

In looksmaxxing communities they are discussed alongside castor oil, microneedling, minoxidil and prescription prostaglandin analogues. Published work centres on prescription bimatoprost applied to brows, while a 2019 paper reported on a plant-derived extract (Jarilla-Coffea) described as improving eyelash and eyebrow growth in women. No trials of peptide serums for brows were found.

paras: The serum is applied to the brows, usually once or twice daily over a period of weeks to months. Users often combine it with castor oil, microneedling or minoxidil. Makers and forum users describe peptides as stimulating follicle activity.
Eye-area products can irritate. Bimatoprost, a prescription drug, has its own documented effects such as eyelid darkening, and findings from bimatoprost studies do not carry over to peptide serums.

angle.text: Users apply peptide or botanical serums to make sparse brows look denser and fuller, often alongside castor oil, microneedling or minoxidil. The idea is that the serum stimulates the brow follicles. Published work centres on prescription bimatoprost rather than over-the-counter products.

lead: Eyebrow growth serums are topical cosmetic products, usually containing peptides or botanical extracts, that are marketed to make sparse brows look denser and fuller. Fuller brows frame the eyes and are a visible part of facial appearance, so people who have thin, over-plucked or patchy brows use these serums as a way to build density over weeks or months rather than drawing it on each day. They are discussed in looksmaxxing communities alongside castor oil, microneedling, minoxidil and prescription prostaglandin analogues.[1][2]

Published research specific to over-the-counter serums is limited. A 2019 paper in Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dermatology reported on a plant-derived extract (Jarilla-Coffea) described as improving eyelash and eyebrow growth in women.[3] Most of the clinical literature on brow growth concerns bimatoprost, a prescription prostaglandin analogue, which has been examined in eyebrow hypotrichosis (sparse eyebrows).[4][5]

Serums sit at the gentlest end of a ladder of options that people use for brows. Cosmetic alternatives that change the look immediately, such as microblading, tattooing and brow powders or pencils, work on a different principle: they add pigment rather than hair, and are covered in the sections below for context.[6]
infobox: Brushed or dabbed onto the brow line

paras: Serums are brushed or dabbed onto the brow area, typically with a small applicator, once or twice a day. Products vary widely, and some contain ingredients that forum users have catalogued from cosmetic-ingredient lists, such as myristoyl pentapeptide-17, myristoyl hexapeptide-16 and octapeptide-2, which supporters describe as stimulating hair-related keratin genes or counteracting inhibitory signals in follicles.

Other products rely on plant extracts, vitamins, conditioning oils and similar ingredients intended to improve the condition of the hair shaft so brows look fuller. Some brands sell a single serum for both lashes and brows; one Singapore-based brow salon chain, for example, sells its own lash and brow serum alongside services such as brow embroidery and lash extensions.[7]

sections.h: Background: eyebrows and why density matters
paras: Eyebrows keep sweat and debris away from the eyes and are an important channel for facial expression; researchers cited on Wikipedia describe communication as their primary function.[8] Because they sit directly above the eyes, brow shape and density strongly influence how a face reads, which is why brow grooming has gone through repeated fashion cycles, from fully removed brows in some historical periods to thin plucked brows in the 1920s and 1930s and fuller brows more recently.[8]

Over-plucking, shaving, ageing, hormonal or medical hair-loss conditions and genetics can all leave brows sparse. Options include waiting for regrowth, drawing brows on with makeup, cosmetic tattooing (microblading, which deposits pigment in the upper dermis and fades over time), hair transplantation of brow follicles, and topical products intended to promote growth.[6][8]

A 2011 report in Dermatologic Surgery examined bimatoprost ophthalmic solution 0.03% for eyebrow growth.[4] Bimatoprost is a prostaglandin F2-alpha analogue approved in the US from 2001 for glaucoma and ocular hypertension; a cosmetic formulation is approved for eyelash hypotrichosis.[2] Wikipedia describes a case report of a 60-year-old woman with eyebrow hypotrichosis who applied a 0.03% solution daily for eight months and was reported to have increased growth and thickening of brow hairs.[2]

A 2020 retrospective study in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology followed 48 patients with eyebrow hypotrichosis treated with bimatoprost 0.01% over 24 weeks, analysing changes in hair density and diameter by part of the brow (head, body, tail).[5] These studies concern a prescription drug rather than over-the-counter serums.

The 2019 Jarilla-Coffea extract paper, whose title reports improved lash and brow growth in women, is the main published study identified of a cosmetic botanical product.[3] No published trial of peptide-based brow serums has been found.

Eye-area products can cause irritation or allergic reactions. For bimatoprost, documented effects include redness and irritation, darkening of the eyelid or skin beneath the eye with the cosmetic formulation, and permanent iris darkening when used as eye drops; reusing single-use applicators has been linked to infection.[2] Cosmetic tattooing carries its own risks, including pigment migration and colour change, infection if equipment is not sterile, and reactions to inks, and the pigment fades so touch-ups are typically scheduled.[6]

A looksmax.org thread lists peptide ingredients and asks members to find a serum containing them; a reply asks for a breakdown of how legitimate each is, and the original poster says they are legitimate but a good product is hard to find. Another thread asks about the best microneedling approach for brow growth. Castor oil is also recommended in forum answers, with one user saying shaved brows return within two to four weeks.

Brow growth is generally treated as one component of a wider 'eyebrowmaxxing' routine that can include grooming shape, tinting, serums and, for some, prescription options discussed with a dermatologist.

lore.intro: Brow-growth products are discussed as part of 'eyebrowmaxxing', often as a stack with other treatments.
